title: Chapter 30: The Eighth Person
html:
He San argued as hard as he could, but his seniors assumed he was exaggerating to excuse his own nerves. They had already spent several minutes inside and, so far, nothing truly frightening had happened.

“Xiao San, if you’re that scared, you can hide behind your big sister.” Sister Hui took the lead and entered the next room alone. “The decorations are good, but I’ve seen crime dramas with more tension than this.”

“Then we’ll use the groups Brother Feng suggested.” Monkey hurried after her. “Let’s find the exit before I get bored.”

Lao Song and a quiet student named Shi Ling followed them, leaving He San with Brother Feng and Lao Zhao in the corridor.

“I’m honestly a little disappointed.” Lao Zhao was a broad, heavyset student who began sweating easily even with light exertion.

“Save your breath. Let’s move.” Brother Feng waved him forward.

For a moment, He San was left alone in the corridor, still the only person treating the attraction as a genuine threat.Something is definitely going to happen.

He took two steps, then stopped.Wait. Did the background music change? Why does this sound familiar?

Before he could concentrate on the music, a faint metallic sound reached him from farther down the corridor. It vanished almost as soon as he noticed it.

Is someone behind us?He San hurried after his seniors rather than stay behind to investigate. With Black Friday playing, Murder by Midnight shifted into its active phase: the lights dimmed, pieces of set dressing seemed to move in the corners of their vision, and chains rattled somewhere near the stairwells.

“I found something!” Sister Hui emerged from a room holding a rag doll. “This was sitting right in the middle of the floor.”

“Senior, maybe don’t move random props. Last time, touching the coffin activated part of the scenario.” He San’s warning went ignored. He remained at the edge of the group, watching his seniors confidently make every choice he wished they would avoid.

“It has to be a clue. Why else put it in the center of the room?” Monkey raised the doll toward the dim light. It resembled a little girl, but its eyes had been removed and the fabric was darkened as though by smoke. “No eyes could mean darkness, and the fire damage could connect to the building’s backstory.”

“Maybe it represents the old fire,” Brother Feng said, gently pressing the doll. “There’s something inside besides stuffing. Check it.”

Monkey opened the zipper on the back. The doll was packed with scraps of paper. He pulled one out and squinted at the uneven, childlike handwriting.

“What does it say?”

Monkey’s expression darkened. He turned the paper toward the group. Six words were scrawled across it: ALL OF YOU HAVE TO DIE!

“Every piece says the same thing.”

“That is an impressive amount of hatred for a prop.”

“Put it back. I don’t like it.” Shi Ling, who had barely spoken until now, took several steps away from the doll.

“It’s just set dressing.” Monkey pushed the papers back inside and tossed the doll into a corner. “Come on. Next room.”

The slight tremor in his voice made his confidence less convincing.

“Wait.” Sister Hui held up a crumpled sheet of paper. “I found this in the same room. It looks like part of a diary.”

“Let me see.” Lao Zhao took it and read aloud. “I think there is another person hiding in our house. Sometimes I wonder whether he is under the bed or inside the cupboard. I told Mom, Dad, and my sister, but they were too busy to listen. At night, Dad checks every door and window before we go to sleep. I don’t understand why they are so afraid of what might be outside when someone is already hiding in here with us.”

“What is this?” Lao Zhao stopped and handed the page back. “It’s written to get inside our heads. Don’t fall for it.”

“The attention to detail is impressive, but it’ll take more than a diary entry to scare me.” Sister Hui returned the paper to where she had found it, and the group continued. None of them noticed the discarded doll twitch in the corner.

“Let’s stop wasting time and find the exit.” After searching five rooms without success, they reached the far end of the corridor.

“This floor is too large to search completely before the timer ends,” Brother Feng reasoned. “I doubt the exit is on the same level as the entrance. If I designed the attraction, I’d force visitors to move between floors.”

“So we split up again?”

“No! If we separate across different floors, it becomes even easier to isolate us!” He San protested, only to be ignored again.

“We’ve been here for more than ten minutes and nothing major has happened. The atmosphere is good, but I’m still not scared.” Lao Zhao wiped his forehead. “Remember why we came. We need to find the exit within the time limit and restore our university’s reputation.”

“Agreed. We’ll split up as planned.”

As the decision was about to become final, He San stepped into the middle of the group. “Will all of you please listen to me for once?”

He pointed down the corridor. “For the last few minutes, I’ve been hearing something near the stairwell. I think something is following us.”

Once he said it aloud, the others finally noticed the faint clinking of chains growing closer.

“The scenario is called Murder by Midnight, so obviously there’s supposed to be a murderer,” Lao Zhao said, patting He San on the shoulder. “That just means an employee in costume. Why are you worrying so much?”

The others laughed, convinced that He San was being overly sensitive.

“Relax. Your seniors will protect you.” Lao Zhao took out his phone. “Besides, didn’t we agree to film a short video in here and post it on the boss’s page? This spot is perfect. Everyone look at the camera.”

He adjusted the angle to fit the entire group into frame. Then he glanced at the screen—and went completely still.

His hand began to tremble, and the phone slipped from his fingers.

“Fatty! What’s wrong with you?”

“You nearly scared me!”

Lao Zhao said nothing at first. He counted the faces around him again, then stammered, “Count for yourselves. Including me… why are there eight people here?”
